notes.front: What are human factors, in one of the handbook’s definitions?
notes.back: The elements that affect our behaviour and performance, especially those that may cause us to make errors.
notes.explanation: Fatigue, complacency and stress are examples; the handbook notes human factors exist in both proper and improper actions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Definitions of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: Human factors are those elements that affect our behavior and performance, especially those that may cause us to make errors.
notes.example: Like the reasons a careful driver still misses a turning when tired or distracted, but applied to aircraft maintenance.

notes.front: What is the FAA Safety Team (FAASTeam) website a source of?
notes.back: Up-to-date information on safety concerns, upcoming seminars, featured courses and resources, at www.faasafety.gov.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists it among the places to get information on human factors.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “FAA Safety Team”, p. 14-31
notes.evidence: The FAA Safety Team has a dedicated website that provides up-to-date information safety concerns, upcoming seminars, featured courses and resources.
notes.example: Like a club noticeboard for safety seminars and courses, but run online by the regulator.

notes.front: In maintenance human factors, what is the overall research goal concerning human performance?
notes.back: To identify and optimise the factors that affect human performance in maintenance and inspection.
notes.explanation: The ACS lists human performance and limitations as a knowledge element; people do not all share the same capabilities or limitations.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Elements of Human Factors”, p. 14-2
notes.evidence: The overall goal of aviation maintenance human factors research is to identify and optimize the factors that affect human performance in maintenance and inspection.
notes.example: Like a coach studying what helps or hinders each athlete, but for technicians at work.

notes.front: What shift in focus began the evolution of maintenance human factors in World War I?
notes.back: From the pilot onto the aircraft, especially the design of controls and displays, altitude and environmental effects.
notes.explanation: More sophisticated equipment, which personnel could not always use, raised interest in human capability.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Evolution of Maintenance Human Factors”, p. 14-7
notes.evidence: Up to this point, the focus of aviation psychology was on the pilot, but as time progressed, the focus shifted onto the aircraft.
notes.example: Like moving from choosing drivers who can cope with any car to designing cars that suit drivers.

notes.front: What is the PEAR model?
notes.back: A memory jogger for four considerations of maintenance human factors programmes: People, Environment, Actions and Resources.
notes.explanation: It gives a unified, practical view of what to be concerned about in maintenance human factors.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “The Pear Model”, p. 14-9
notes.evidence: For more than a decade, the term “PEAR” has been used as a memory jogger, or mnemonic, to characterize human factors in aviation maintenance.
notes.example: Like a checklist acronym for packing a bag, but for designing safe maintenance work.

notes.front: What is the Dirty Dozen?
notes.back: Twelve human factors, identified by Transport Canada, that degrade people’s ability to perform effectively and safely and could lead to maintenance errors.
notes.explanation: The industry adopted them as a straightforward way to discuss human error in maintenance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “The “Dirty Dozen””, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: Transport Canada identified twelve human factors that degrade people’s ability to perform effectively and safely, which could lead to maintenance errors.
notes.example: Like a list of the twelve most common causes of kitchen accidents, used to train new cooks.

notes.front: What is lack of communication, as a Dirty Dozen factor?
notes.back: A key human factor that can result in suboptimal, incorrect or faulty maintenance.
notes.explanation: Communication happens with management, pilots, suppliers and servicers, but between technicians it may be the most important.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Communication”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: Lack of communication is a key human factor that can result in suboptimal, incorrect, or faulty maintenance.
notes.example: Like a relay runner dropping the baton because nobody said which hand to pass it to.

notes.front: What is complacency, as a Dirty Dozen factor?
notes.back: A sense of self satisfaction and false confidence that typically develops over time as knowledge and experience grow.
notes.explanation: A repetitive inspection item may be skipped because it has never shown a fault.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Complacency”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: As a technician gains knowledge and experience, a sense of self satisfaction and false confidence may occur.
notes.example: Like no longer checking your mirrors on a road you drive every day.

notes.front: What can lack of knowledge lead to in aircraft maintenance?
notes.back: A faulty repair that can have catastrophic results.
notes.explanation: Technology differs between aircraft and changes on a single aircraft, so the required knowledge is hard to keep up.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Knowledge”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: A lack of knowledge when performing aircraft maintenance can result in a faulty repair that can have catastrophic results.
notes.example: Like fitting a part from memory of a different car model and finding it works differently.

notes.front: How does a distraction cause maintenance errors?
notes.back: It disrupts the procedure, and on resuming the technician may skip a detail that needs attention.
notes.explanation: Distractions can be mental or physical, from the hangar or from personal worries.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Distraction”, p. 14-15
notes.evidence: A distraction while performing maintenance on an aircraft may disrupt the procedure. [Figure 14-21] When work resumes, it is possible that the technician skips over a detail that needs attention.
notes.example: Like losing your place in a recipe after a phone call and forgetting the salt.

notes.front: What does teamwork involve, the lack of which is a Dirty Dozen factor?
notes.back: Everyone understanding and agreeing on the actions to be taken.
notes.explanation: A lack of teamwork makes all jobs harder and could cause a miscommunication affecting airworthiness.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Teamwork”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: Often associated with improved safety in the workplace, teamwork involves everyone understanding and agreeing on actions to be taken.
notes.example: Like a pit crew where each member knows the plan before the car arrives.

notes.front: When is a person said to be fatigued?
notes.back: When cognitive ability, decision-making, reaction time, coordination, speed, strength or balance is reduced or impaired.
notes.explanation: Fatigue can be mental, physical or emotional, and the handbook calls it a major human factor in maintenance errors.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: A person is said to be fatigued when a reduction or impairment in any of the following occurs: cognitive ability, decision-making, reaction time, coordination, speed, strength, or balance.
notes.example: Like driving home after a night shift: you may feel fine yet react more slowly.

notes.front: How does lack of resources interfere with a maintenance task?
notes.back: A lack of supplies and support, or low-quality products, affects a person’s ability to complete it.
notes.explanation: Maintenance demands proper tools and parts; any lack can cause non-fatal and fatal accidents.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Resources”, p. 14-18
notes.evidence: A lack of resources can interfere with a person’s ability to complete a task because of a lack of supplies and support.
notes.example: Like trying to change a tyre without the right wheel brace.

notes.front: What is pressure, as a Dirty Dozen factor?
notes.back: Constant pressure to do things better and faster without mistakes, which can affect workers’ capability to do the job right.
notes.explanation: Airlines’ strict finances and tight schedules push mechanics to find and fix problems quickly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pressure”, p. 14-22
notes.evidence: Aviation maintenance tasks require individuals to perform in an environment with constant pressure to do things better and faster without making mistakes
notes.example: Like being told the aircraft must leave in twenty minutes while you are still torquing bolts.

notes.front: What is assertiveness, the lack of which is a Dirty Dozen factor?
notes.back: The ability to express feelings, opinions, beliefs and needs in a positive, productive manner; it is not aggression.
notes.explanation: Technicians who do not voice concerns about a repair could ultimately cost people their lives.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Assertiveness”, p. 14-22
notes.evidence: Assertiveness is the ability to express your feelings, opinions, beliefs, and needs in a positive, productive manner and should not be confused with being aggressive.
notes.example: Like telling a colleague calmly, with facts, that a shortcut worries you.

notes.front: What is stress, as the handbook’s Dirty Dozen figure defines it?
notes.back: The subconscious response to the demands placed on a person.
notes.explanation: Short timeframes, changing technology, dark tight spaces and long hours make maintenance stressful.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Stress”, p. 14-27
notes.evidence: Stress is the subconscious response to the demands placed on a person.
notes.example: Like the tension of a deadline, but where a mistake could cost lives.

notes.front: How does the handbook define lack of awareness?
notes.back: A failure to recognise all the consequences of an action, or lack of foresight.
notes.explanation: After doing the same task many times, technicians can become less vigilant about what they do and what is around them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Awareness”, p. 14-26
notes.evidence: Lack of awareness is defined as a failure to recognize all the consequences of an action or lack of foresight.
notes.example: Like refitting a panel without noticing it now covers a new modification.

notes.front: What are norms, as a Dirty Dozen factor?
notes.back: Short for “normal”: the unwritten rules for how things are normally done, followed or tolerated by most organisations.
notes.explanation: Negative norms can detract from the established safety standard and cause an accident.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Norms”, p. 14-26
notes.evidence: Norms is short for “normal,” or the way things are normally done. [Figure 14-31] They are unwritten rules that are followed or tolerated by most organizations.
notes.example: Like a workshop habit of skipping a step “because we always do”.

notes.front: What happens at a shift turnover in maintenance?
notes.back: A partially completed job passes from the technician finishing their day to the one coming on duty.
notes.explanation: Many completed steps cannot be seen once components hide them, so the departing technician must explain the work thoroughly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Communication”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: A partially completed job is transferred from the technician finishing their workday to the technician coming on duty.
notes.example: Like a nurse’s handover at the end of a ward shift.

notes.front: What is a safe culture, in the handbook’s words?
notes.back: One where there is a shared value and attitude toward safety.
notes.explanation: In a safe culture each person understands their own role contributes to overall mission safety.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Organizational”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: A safe culture is one where there is a shared value and attitude toward safety.
notes.example: Like a team where anyone may stop the line when they see a hazard.

notes.front: In event investigation with the Maintenance Error Decision Aid, what is the goal?
notes.back: To investigate errors, understand root causes and prevent accidents, not simply blame maintenance personnel.
notes.explanation: The Boeing-developed aid assumes errors result from a series of factors; the ACS lists event investigation as a knowledge element.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Resources”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: The goal of using MEDA is to investigate errors, understand root causes, and prevent accidents, instead of simply placing blame on the maintenance personnel for the errors.
notes.example: Like an air accident report that asks why the error happened rather than who to punish.

notes.front: Where does the ACS list conditions and preconditions for unsafe acts?
notes.back: As a knowledge element of the Human Factors area.
notes.explanation: The ACS names it without defining it; the handbook’s nearest material is latent failures, decisions made long before an incident.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.K10 Conditions/preconditions for unsafe acts. AM.I.L.K11 Types of human errors.
uses: conditions and preconditions for unsafe acts
introduces: conditions and preconditions for unsafe acts
notes.example: Like a broken ladder left in the hangar: not the fall itself, but what set it up.

notes.front: What is maintenance resource management (MRM) in the handbook?
notes.back: A human factors term listed beside crew resource management in Figure 14-1; the handbook gives no fuller definition.
notes.explanation: Its history section does describe crew-resource-management-style maintenance training in the 1990s, aimed at communication and teamwork.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Human Factors (Figure 14-1)”, p. 14-2
notes.evidence: Instructional Systems Design Latent Failure Leadership Maintenance Resource Management Mental Model Norms
notes.example: Like crew resource management on the flight deck, but for maintenance teams.

notes.front: In the handbook’s discussion of norms, what should technicians take pride in?
notes.back: Following procedure, rather than unsafe norms that may have been adopted as regular practice.
notes.explanation: The ACS lists professionalism and integrity as a Human Factors knowledge element.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Norms”, p. 14-27
notes.evidence: AMTs should pride themselves on following procedure, rather than unsafe norms that may have been adopted as regular practice.
notes.example: Like a pilot running the full checklist even when colleagues skip it.

notes.front: Accident data show that approximately {{c1::75–80}} percent of all aviation accidents result from human error.
notes.back: 75–80 percent.
notes.explanation: Of those accidents, about 12 percent are maintenance related.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Importance of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: A review of accident related data indicates that approximately 75–80 percent of all aviation accidents are the result of human error. Of those accidents, about 12 percent are maintenance related.

notes.front: Of accidents caused by human error, about what share are maintenance related?
notes.back: About 12 percent.
notes.explanation: Maintenance errors tend to be more latent and less obvious than pilot errors, but can be just as lethal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Importance of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: Of those accidents, about 12 percent are maintenance related.

notes.front: What share of maintenance errors does the handbook say it is universally agreed involve human factors?
notes.back: 80 percent.
notes.explanation: Undetected, they can cause events, worker injuries, wasted time and even accidents.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Definitions of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: It is universally agreed that 80 percent of maintenance errors involve human factors.

notes.front: How does the handbook define human error?
notes.back: The unintentional act of performing a task incorrectly that can potentially degrade the system.
notes.explanation: Improper actions usually result in human error.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Definitions of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: Human error is the unintentional act of performing a task incorrectly that can potentially degrade the system.

notes.front: Which type of human error is not performing an act or task?
notes.back: Omission.
notes.explanation: It is one of three types, with commission and extraneous.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Definitions of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: There are three types of human error: 1. Omission: not performing an act or task.

notes.front: Which type of human error is accomplishing a task incorrectly?
notes.back: Commission.
notes.explanation: Omission leaves the task undone; commission does it wrongly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Definitions of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: 2. Commission: accomplishing a task incorrectly.

notes.front: Which type of human error is performing a task not authorised?
notes.back: Extraneous.
notes.explanation: It completes the handbook’s three types of human error.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Definitions of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: 3. Extraneous: performing a task not authorized.

notes.front: According to the handbook, when do human factors usually create a problem that contributes to an accident?
notes.back: In most cases, when three or four of the factors combine.
notes.explanation: Some factors are more serious than others on their own.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Introduction”, p. 14-2
notes.evidence: Some are more serious than others but, in most cases, when you combine three or four of the factors, they create a problem that contributes to an accident or incident.

notes.front: Which human factors discipline studies the dimensions and abilities of the human body?
notes.back: Anthropometry.
notes.explanation: It matters because of the confined spaces technicians work in and the size of tools.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Anthropometry”, p. 14-4
notes.evidence: Anthropometry is the study of the dimensions and abilities of the human body.

notes.front: Which human factors discipline is the organised approach to the study of work?
notes.back: Industrial engineering.
notes.explanation: Unrealistic work standards create unnecessary stressors that cause mistakes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Industrial Engineering”, p. 14-5
notes.evidence: Industrial engineering is the organized approach to the study of work.

notes.front: What did the Hawthorne Effect suggest?
notes.back: That motivational factors could significantly influence human performance.
notes.explanation: It came from studies of the effects of illumination on worker productivity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Evolution of Maintenance Human Factors”, p. 14-7
notes.evidence: This led to the identification of the Hawthorne Effect, which suggested that motivational factors could significantly influence human performance.

notes.front: What did Continental Airlines begin in maintenance in 1991?
notes.back: Crew-resource-management-style training, to improve communication, teamwork and participative decision making.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives it as one example of the 1990s culture change at American carriers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Evolution of Maintenance Human Factors”, p. 14-9
notes.evidence: One example is in 1991, when Continental Airlines began “CRM type” training in maintenance. They saw the importance of improving communication, teamwork, and participative decision making.

notes.front: In the PEAR model, what must the company match to the tasks each person performs?
notes.back: The physical characteristics of each person, such as size, strength, age and eyesight.
notes.explanation: Identical standards cannot be applied equally to all employees.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “People”, p. 14-9
notes.evidence: The company must match the physical characteristics of each person to the tasks each performs.

notes.front: What are the two environments the PEAR model’s “E” covers?
notes.back: The physical workplace and the organisational environment within the company.
notes.explanation: A human factors programme must pay attention to both.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Environment”, p. 14-9
notes.evidence: There are at least two environments in aviation maintenance. There is the physical workplace on the ramp, in the hangar, or in the shop. In addition, there is the organizational environment that exists within the company.

notes.front: Under “Actions” in PEAR, what is the standard approach to identifying the knowledge, skills and attitudes each task needs?
notes.back: Job task analysis.
notes.explanation: It also shows what instructions, tools and other resources are needed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Actions”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: Job task analysis (JTA) is the standard human factors approach to identify the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to perform each task in a given job.

notes.front: In PEAR, how broadly is a “resource” defined?
notes.back: Anything a technician, or anyone else, needs to get the job done.
notes.explanation: Examples range from protective clothing and rivets to staff numbers and time.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Resources”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: A resource is anything a technician (or anyone else) needs to get the job done.

notes.front: What are the three principles the Maintenance Error Decision Aid is based on?
notes.back: Positive employee intent, contribution of multiple factors, and manageability of errors.
notes.explanation: Technicians are assumed to want to do the best job and not to err intentionally.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Resources”, p. 14-11
notes.evidence: Positive employee intent (In other words, maintenance technicians want to do the best job possible and do not make intentional errors.) • Contribution of multiple factors

notes.front: What is the final step of the Maintenance Error Decision Aid process?
notes.back: Feedback: technicians are told that changes have been made to the maintenance system.
notes.explanation: It follows prevention strategies, which are reviewed, prioritised, implemented and tracked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Resources”, p. 14-11
notes.evidence: 5. Feedback: the operator provides feedback to the maintenance workplace so technicians know that changes have been made to the maintenance system as a result of this MEDA process.

notes.front: In James Reason’s Swiss cheese model, when can an incident take place?
notes.back: Only when the “holes” in the different systems are all aligned.
notes.explanation: It is his Model of Accident Causation, introduced in 1990.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Human Factors”, p. 14-12
notes.evidence: Only when the holes are all aligned can the incident take place.

notes.front: In Reason’s model, what is an active failure?
notes.back: One whose effects are immediate.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s example is an aircraft slipping off a jack placed wrongly by the technician.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Human Factors”, p. 14-12
notes.evidence: An active failure is one in which the effects are immediate.

notes.front: In Reason’s model, what is a latent failure?
notes.back: One resulting from a decision or action made long before the incident; its consequences may lie dormant for a long time.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s example is an unapproved jack used because funding was not approved.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Human Factors”, p. 14-12
notes.evidence: A latent failure occurs as a result of a decision or action made long before the incident or accident actually occurs.

notes.front: Within unintentional errors, what is a slip and what is a mistake?
notes.back: A slip is an error in action; a mistake is an error in opinion or judgement from poor reasoning, carelessness or insufficient knowledge.
notes.explanation: Both are accidental deviations from accuracy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Errors”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: This can include an error in your action (a slip), opinion, or judgment caused by poor reasoning, carelessness, or insufficient knowledge (a mistake).

notes.front: In aviation maintenance, what should an intentional error really be considered?
notes.back: A violation: a purposeful deviation from safe practices, procedures, standards or regulations.
notes.explanation: The person knowingly chooses to do something wrong.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Errors”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: In aviation maintenance, an intentional error should really be considered a violation.

notes.front: Is human error avoidable, according to the handbook?
notes.back: No, but it is manageable.
notes.explanation: Training and inspections should make errors visible before they produce damaging consequences.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Human Error”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: Simply put, human error is not avoidable but it is manageable.

notes.front: Among all the people technicians communicate with, whose communication may be the most important?
notes.back: Communication between technicians.
notes.explanation: It is especially critical where more than one technician works on the aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Communication”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: But communication between AMTs may be the most important of all.

notes.front: Before continuing a job someone else started, what communication must there be?
notes.back: Both oral and written communication between the technician who started it and the one continuing it.
notes.explanation: Ideally a face-to-face meeting; a phone call can give the oral turnover if needed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Communication”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: It is vital that work not be continued on a project without both oral and written communication between the technician who started the job and the technician continuing it.

notes.front: What behaviour is a sign that complacency may exist?
notes.back: Performing work without documentation, or documenting work that was not performed.
notes.explanation: Proper paperwork draws attention to a work item and reinforces its significance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Complacency”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: When a technician performs work without documentation, or documents work that was not performed, it is a sign that complacency may exist.

notes.front: To combat complacency, what must a technician be trained to expect?
notes.back: To find the fault that created the inspection item in the first place.
notes.explanation: All inspection items must be treated with equal importance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Complacency”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: To combat complacency, a technician must be trained to expect to find the fault that created the inspection item in the first place.

notes.front: When in doubt about a procedure, whom should a technician consult first, and whom if that fails?
notes.back: A technician experienced on the aircraft; failing that, a manufacturer’s technical representative.
notes.explanation: It is better to delay maintenance than do it incorrectly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Knowledge”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: When in doubt, a technician with experience

notes.front: About what share of maintenance related errors are estimated to be caused by distractions?
notes.back: 15 percent.
notes.explanation: Distractions can be mental or physical, in the work area or in the technician’s mind.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Distraction”, p. 14-15
notes.evidence: It is estimated that 15 percent of maintenance related errors are caused by distractions.

notes.front: After a distraction, from where does the handbook suggest resuming the job?
notes.back: Go back three steps in the procedure from where the distraction occurred.
notes.explanation: Signing off each step only once complete also helps.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Distraction”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: A good practice is to go back three steps in the work procedure from when distraction occurred and resume the job from that point.

notes.front: What is the primary cause of fatigue?
notes.back: A lack of sleep.
notes.explanation: Stress and overworking can also cause fatigue.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: The primary cause of fatigue is a lack of sleep.

notes.front: How many hours of daily sleep does the handbook recommend to avoid fatigue?
notes.back: Eight to nine hours.
notes.explanation: The best remedy for fatigue is enough sleep on a regular basis.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-17
notes.evidence: Eight to nine hours of daily sleep are recommended to avoid fatigue.

notes.front: What is circadian rhythm?
notes.back: The daily rise and fall of variables such as body temperature, heart rate, alertness and attention.
notes.explanation: Working counter to it can be difficult, so complex tasks are avoided at its bottom.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: Variables such as body temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, blood chemistry, alertness, and attention rise and fall in a pattern daily. This is known as circadian rhythm.

notes.front: Is a fatigued person usually aware of it?
notes.back: Not necessarily: until it becomes extreme they may be unaware; others or the results of tasks show it more easily.
notes.explanation: A fatigued person may even feel wide awake.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: Until it becomes extreme, a person may be unaware that they are fatigued. It is easier recognized by another person or in the results of tasks being performed.

notes.front: According to the handbook, how much time off during a week of work does 14 CFR 121.377 require?
notes.back: Only 24 hours.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this obviously not enough, leaving companies and technicians to regulate shift work and time off.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-18
notes.evidence: Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 121, section 377, only requires 24 hours time off during a week of work.

notes.front: What does the maintenance term “aircraft on ground” indicate?
notes.back: A problem serious enough to prevent an aircraft from flying.
notes.explanation: There is then a rush to get parts to return the aircraft to service.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Resources”, p. 14-19
notes.evidence: Aircraft on ground (AOG) is a term in aviation maintenance indicating that a problem is serious enough to prevent an aircraft from flying.

notes.front: If tools are broken, out of calibration or missing, what does the handbook say must happen?
notes.back: They must be repaired, calibrated or found as soon as possible.
notes.explanation: The right tools for the job need to be used at all times.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Resources”, p. 14-21
notes.evidence: calibration, or missing, they need to be repaired, calibrated, or found as soon as possible.

notes.front: What is self-induced pressure?
notes.back: Taking ownership of a situation that was not of your doing.
notes.explanation: The remedies include asking for help and having someone check the repair.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pressure”, p. 14-22
notes.evidence: Self-induced pressures are those occasions where one takes ownership of a situation that was not of their doing.

notes.front: What is the first step the handbook gives for offsetting a lack of assertiveness?
notes.back: Address managers and supervisors directly by stating the problem.
notes.explanation: Then explain the consequences, propose solutions and solicit feedback.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Assertiveness”, p. 14-22
notes.evidence: 1. Address managers and supervisors directly by stating the problem.

notes.front: Into which three categories are stressors grouped?
notes.back: Physical, psychological and physiological.
notes.explanation: The causes of stress are called stressors.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Stress”, p. 14-24
notes.evidence: The causes of stress are referred to as “stressors” and are categorized as physical, psychological, or physiological.

notes.front: What are two physiological stressors?
notes.back: Any two of fatigue, poor physical condition, hunger and disease.
notes.explanation: Conflicting shift schedules and lack of sleep appear among them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Physiological Stressors”, p. 14-25
notes.evidence: Physiological stressors include fatigue, poor physical condition, hunger, and disease.

notes.front: According to specialists, what is the first step in coping with stress?
notes.back: Identify the stressors and the symptoms that follow exposure to them.
notes.explanation: A healthy lifestyle with rest, exercise and diet is also recommended.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Stress”, p. 14-26
notes.evidence: Specialists say that the first step is to identify stressors and the symptoms that occur after exposure to those stressors.

notes.front: To counter lack of awareness, how must each repeated task be treated?
notes.back: As if it were the first time.
notes.explanation: Repetition makes technicians less vigilant about what they do and what is around them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Awareness”, p. 14-26
notes.evidence: Each time a task is completed it must be treated as if it were the first time.

notes.front: What are two examples of unsafe norms?
notes.back: Any two of taking shortcuts, working from memory and not following procedures.
notes.explanation: Unsafe norms are non-productive or detract from the group’s productivity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Norms”, p. 14-27
notes.evidence: aircraft maintenance, working from memory, or not following procedures are examples of unsafe norms.

notes.front: Who are better able to identify unsafe norms: newcomers or long-standing group members?
notes.back: Newcomers.
notes.explanation: But a newcomer’s credibility depends on assimilation into the group, which depends on following its norms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Norms”, p. 14-27
notes.evidence: Newcomers are better able to identify these unsafe norms than long-standing members of the group.

notes.front: What are two of the most common maintenance errors found by the United Kingdom Civil Aviation Authority?
notes.back: Any two of: incorrect installation of components, wrong parts, wiring discrepancies, forgotten tools and parts, failure to lubricate, among others.
notes.explanation: The handbook says all can be avoided by following the job card procedures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Example of Common Maintenance Errors”, p. 14-28
notes.evidence: 1. Incorrect installation of components. 2. Fitting of wrong parts. 3. Electrical wiring discrepancies to include crossing connections.

notes.front: Historically, what share of accidents does the handbook attribute to machine failure and what share to human factors?
notes.back: Twenty percent machine failure; eighty percent human factors.
notes.explanation: Human factors awareness began with pilots and has spread to maintenance training.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Example of Common Maintenance Errors”, p. 14-29
notes.evidence: Historically, twenty percent of all accidents are caused by a machine failure, and eighty percent by human factors.

notes.front: What happens to accident likelihood if the chain of events is broken at the maintenance level?
notes.back: It can be drastically decreased.
notes.explanation: Incident reviews show a series of human errors building until the accident occurred.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Example of Common Maintenance Errors”, p. 14-29
notes.evidence: If the chain of events is broken at the maintenance level, the likelihood of the accident occurring can be drastically decreased.

notes.front: What is the most direct link for aviation maintenance human factors, according to the handbook?
notes.back: The FAA Human Factors website at hf.faa.gov.
notes.explanation: It holds most of the FAA maintenance human factors documents since 1988.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)”, p. 14-30
notes.evidence: The most direct link for aviation maintenance human factors is the FAA Human Factors website at hf.faa.gov.

notes.front: Which ACS risk management element concerns fatigue?
notes.back: Fatigue management and fitness for duty.
notes.explanation: The applicant must identify, assess and mitigate the associated risks.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.R2 Fatigue management and fitness for duty.

notes.front: Which ACS Human Factors risk element concerns reporting hazards?
notes.back: Selective reporting of hazards.
notes.explanation: Communication and reporting of hazards is also listed as a Human Factors knowledge element.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.R1 Selective reporting of hazards.

notes.front: Which report must an applicant be able to file under the ACS Human Factors skills?
notes.back: A Malfunction or Defect Report.
notes.explanation: The other Human Factors skills are briefing a shift turnover and locating human factors error information.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.S1 File a Malfunction or Defect Report.

notes.front: Which shift-related skill does the ACS require in Human Factors?
notes.back: Brief a shift turnover for continuity of work.
notes.explanation: Shift and task turnover is also listed as a Human Factors knowledge element.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.S2 Brief a shift turnover for continuity of work.

notes.front: In a safe culture, what does each person understand?
notes.back: That their individual role contributes to overall mission safety.
notes.explanation: The best companies guide and support their people and foster a culture of safety.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Organizational”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: In a safe culture, each person understands their individual role is contributing to overall mission safety.

notes.front: What must a technician never sign for?
notes.back: Any work that has not been performed.
notes.explanation: Read the item and confirm it has been done before the pen touches the paper.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Complacency”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: A technician should never sign for any work that has not been performed.

notes.front: At 2200, a technician halfway through a flap actuator change must hand over to the night shift and is running late. What should happen?
notes.back: D: A face-to-face turnover reviewing the paperwork, completed work and next step.
notes.explanation: The handbook says continuing someone else’s job should follow a face-to-face meeting, with the paperwork reviewed and the next step pointed out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Communication”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: Continuing a job that has been started by someone else should only occur after a face-to-face meeting of technicians. The applicable paperwork should be reviewed, the completed work discussed, and attention drawing to the next step.
notes.choices:
A) Leave a sticky note on the aircraft
B) Let the next shift start again from the manual
C) Sign off the whole task so it is not forgotten
D) A face-to-face turnover reviewing the paperwork, completed work and next step
notes.choicesExplained: A gives no oral turnover. B wastes work and ignores hidden completed steps. C signs for work not performed.

notes.front: A technician has checked one fuel filter bowl hundreds of times without finding a fault, and now signs it off without looking. Which Dirty Dozen factor is this?
notes.back: D: Complacency.
notes.explanation: Repeated fault-free checks breed false confidence, so the item is skipped: the handbook’s description of complacency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Complacency”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: A repetitive task, especially an inspection item, may be overlooked or skipped because the technician has performed the task a number of times without ever finding a fault.
notes.choices:
A) Lack of knowledge
B) Stress
C) Lack of resources
D) Complacency
notes.choicesExplained: A would mean not knowing how. C would mean missing tools or parts. B is a response to demands, not overconfidence.

notes.front: A technician experienced on one manufacturer’s aircraft assumes another type’s spoiler lockout works the same way and does not check the manual. Which factor is chiefly at work?
notes.back: C: Lack of knowledge.
notes.explanation: Differences exist in design and procedures between aircraft, and technicians must use the latest data for each type.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Knowledge”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: They must also be aware that differences exist in the design and maintenance procedures on different aircraft.
notes.choices:
A) Norms
B) Distraction
C) Lack of knowledge
D) Fatigue
notes.choicesExplained: A is a group habit. B interrupts a task. D impairs a tired person; none is the missing type knowledge.

notes.front: Midway through reconnecting a fuel line, a technician is called away to move a tug. Returning, they are unsure where they stopped. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: A: Go back three steps in the procedure and resume from there.
notes.explanation: Going back three steps guards against skipping a detail missed during the interruption.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Distraction”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: The technician must recognize when attention to the job at hand is being diverted and assure that work continues correctly.
notes.choices:
A) Go back three steps in the procedure and resume from there
B) Carry on from the step they remember
C) Sign off the task as complete
D) Start a new work card
notes.choicesExplained: B risks the skipped detail. C signs for unverified work. D loses the record of steps done.

notes.front: A technician must leave a partly installed component when the end of shift arrives unexpectedly. What does the handbook suggest to show it is incomplete?
notes.back: B: Disconnect a connector and leave it plainly visible, or tag the work.
notes.explanation: People tend to think a job is finished when a component is “hooked up”, so a visible disconnected connector or tag shows otherwise.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Distraction”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: Disconnect any connector and leave it plainly visible if an installation is not complete.
notes.choices:
A) Tighten everything so it looks finished
B) Disconnect a connector and leave it plainly visible, or tag the work
C) Leave no mark so as not to confuse others
D) Remove the logbook entry
notes.choicesExplained: A creates a false impression of completion. C and D remove the warning or the record.

notes.front: After two nights of poor sleep, a technician feels alert thanks to strong coffee and is about to start a complex rigging task at 0300. What does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: B: Avoid complex tasks at the bottom of the circadian rhythm and have work checked.
notes.explanation: Countermeasures such as caffeine can be short lived while the fatigue remains; complex tasks at the circadian low should be avoided.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-17
notes.evidence: Have others check your work, even if an inspector sign off is not required. Avoid complex tasks during the bottom of your circadian rhythm.
notes.choices:
A) Continue; caffeine removes fatigue
B) Avoid complex tasks at the bottom of the circadian rhythm and have work checked
C) Take more pseudoephedrine to stay sharp
D) Work alone to avoid distraction
notes.choicesExplained: A mistakes a short-lived countermeasure for rest. D: working alone when fatigued is particularly dangerous. C is another countermeasure the handbook warns about.

notes.front: A technician realises they have had far too little sleep and errors seem likely on today’s maintenance. What does the handbook say is justified?
notes.back: B: Time off.
notes.explanation: Time off is justified when too little sleep has occurred and errors are probable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: Time off is justified when too little sleep has occurred and errors are probable during maintenance.
notes.choices:
A) Working faster to finish early
B) Time off
C) Relying on caffeine all shift
D) Skipping documentation to save effort
notes.choicesExplained: A and D add risk. C only masks fatigue for a short time.

notes.front: The correct jacking adapters are missing, and a supervisor suggests improvising with wooden blocks to weigh an aircraft on time. What is the handbook’s view?
notes.back: A: Use the right tools at all times; improvising can be very costly.
notes.explanation: The right tools must be used at all times; the handbook’s load-cell example shows a jack point creasing a spar.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Resources”, p. 14-20
notes.evidence: Having the correct tools means not having to improvise.
notes.choices:
A) Use the right tools at all times; improvising can be very costly
B) Improvise, then note it in the logbook
C) Improvise if the aircraft is light
D) Improvise only on night shift
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D all accept the improvisation the handbook warns against.

notes.front: A manager gives a technician a repair deadline the technician thinks is unrealistic and compromises safety. What should the technician do?
notes.back: D: Bring it to management’s attention and openly discuss another course of action.
notes.explanation: The handbook advises raising unrealistic or unsafe time limits with management and discussing a different course.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pressure”, p. 14-22
notes.evidence: if given a repair with a specific time limitation that you feel is unrealistic or compromises safety, bring it to the attention of the organization’s management and openly discuss a different course of action.
notes.choices:
A) Sign off steps early to save time
B) Skip the less important steps
C) Work unpaid overtime without telling anyone
D) Bring it to management’s attention and openly discuss another course of action
notes.choicesExplained: B and A sacrifice quality and safety for time. C hides the problem and invites fatigue.

notes.front: A technician believes a rushed repair will make a part fail early. Which statement shows assertiveness as the handbook describes it?
notes.back: C: “I have a concern: if we continue, this part will fail sooner. Could we try another way?”.
notes.explanation: It states the problem, explains the consequence and proposes a solution, in a positive, productive manner.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Assertiveness”, p. 14-23
notes.evidence: 3. Propose possible solutions to the problem.
notes.choices:
A) Saying nothing to avoid conflict
B) Shouting that management never listens
C) “I have a concern: if we continue, this part will fail sooner. Could we try another way?”
D) Quietly doing it their own way
notes.choicesExplained: A is a lack of assertiveness. B is aggression. D avoids the discussion altogether.

notes.front: A technician is struggling at work because of an impending divorce and mortgage worries. Which kind of stressor is this?
notes.back: C: Psychological.
notes.explanation: Psychological stressors relate to emotional factors such as family, financial and relationship worries.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Psychological Stressors”, p. 14-24
notes.evidence: Psychological stressors relate to emotional factors, such as a death or illness in the family; business worries; poor interpersonal relationships with family, co-workers, or supervisors; and financial worries.
notes.choices:
A) Physical
B) Physiological
C) Psychological
D) Environmental
notes.choicesExplained: A covers heat, noise, lighting and space. B covers fatigue, hunger and illness. D is not one of the handbook’s three categories.

notes.front: A new technician notices the crew routinely torque bolts from memory instead of the manual. The crew say “that’s how we do it here.” What is this?
notes.back: A: An unsafe norm that supervisors should not tolerate.
notes.explanation: Working from memory is an unsafe norm; supervisors must make everyone follow the same standard.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Norms”, p. 14-27
notes.evidence: Supervisors need to ensure that everyone adheres to the same standards and that unsafe norms are not tolerated.
notes.choices:
A) An unsafe norm that supervisors should not tolerate
B) A healthy norm
C) A lack of resources
D) Acceptable if no one has been hurt
notes.choicesExplained: B mislabels it. C would need missing tools or parts. D confuses luck with safety.

notes.front: A technician refits an access panel exactly as always, not noticing a recent repair nearby that the panel now conflicts with. Which factor, and what mitigation?
notes.back: B: Lack of awareness; check for conflicts with existing modifications or repairs.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s mitigation for lack of awareness is to check whether the work conflicts with an existing modification or repair.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Awareness”, p. 14-28
notes.evidence: Check to see if what you are working on conflicts with an existing modification or repair.
notes.choices:
A) Pressure; ask for more time
B) Lack of awareness; check for conflicts with existing modifications or repairs
C) Fatigue; sleep more
D) Lack of teamwork; hold a meeting
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D name factors whose causes are not in the scenario.

notes.front: Three technicians perform a landing gear swing, each watching a different area, and afterwards agree whether the gear is airworthy. What does this illustrate?
notes.back: B: Teamwork.
notes.explanation: A gear swing involves all team members working together towards a single outcome and forming a consensus.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Teamwork”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: A gear swing or other operational check involves all the members of a team working together.
notes.choices:
A) A norm
B) Teamwork
C) Complacency
D) Distraction
notes.choicesExplained: A is an unwritten habit. C is false confidence. D is an interruption.

notes.front: A company provides portable heaters and better task lighting in a cold, dim hangar. Which PEAR elements does this mainly address?
notes.back: B: Environment, overlapping with Resources.
notes.explanation: The physical environment includes temperature and lighting, and the handbook says providing heaters and lighting overlaps with Resources.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Physical”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: This topic overlaps with the “Resources” component of PEAR when it comes to providing portable heaters, coolers, lighting, clothing, and good workplace and task design.
notes.choices:
A) People only
B) Environment, overlapping with Resources
C) Actions
D) None; it is not human factors
notes.choicesExplained: A focuses on the individual. C is about the tasks performed. D ignores the physical environment.

notes.front: A technician falls because they used a stepladder known to be broken, which management had not replaced. Which is the latent error?
notes.back: C: The broken ladder someone should have replaced.
notes.explanation: The latent error is the company issue leading up to the event; the active error is the obvious event.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Active & Latent”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: An active error is the specific individual activity that is an obvious event. A latent error is the company issues that lead up to the event.
notes.choices:
A) The fall itself
B) The technician choosing to climb
C) The broken ladder someone should have replaced
D) The injury report
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are the active side of the event. D is a record made afterwards.

notes.front: Reading a job card, a technician accidentally transposes a torque value. What kind of error is this?
notes.back: A: Unintentional error (a slip).
notes.explanation: An accidental deviation in action is an unintentional error of the slip type.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Errors”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: An unintentional error is an accidental wandering or deviation from accuracy.
notes.choices:
A) Unintentional error (a slip)
B) Latent failure
C) Extraneous error
D) Intentional violation
notes.choicesExplained: D requires knowingly choosing wrong. B is a decision made long before. C is doing an unauthorised task.

notes.front: Knowing the manual requires a leak check, a technician deliberately skips it to save time. What is this?
notes.back: C: A violation.
notes.explanation: Knowingly choosing to deviate from procedures is a violation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Errors”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: If someone knowingly or intentionally chooses to do something wrong, it is a violation, which means that one has purposely deviated from safe practices, procedures, standards, or regulations.
notes.choices:
A) A slip
B) A mistake from lack of knowledge
C) A violation
D) An omission caused by distraction
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are unintentional. D implies the step was forgotten, not deliberately skipped.

notes.front: After a maintenance-caused incident, a manager wants to find and retrain the technician responsible and close the case. What does the Maintenance Error Decision Aid approach say?
notes.back: B: Look for the factors that contributed to the error, not the employee.
notes.explanation: Blaming the individual leaves contributing factors unchanged, so the mistake is likely to recur.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Resources”, p. 14-11
notes.evidence: In an effort to break this “blame and train” cycle, MEDA investigators learn to look for the factors that contributed to the error, instead of the employee who made the error.
notes.choices:
A) That is the correct approach
B) Look for the factors that contributed to the error, not the employee
C) Suspend the technician first
D) Ignore it if nobody was hurt
notes.choicesExplained: A is the “blame and train” cycle the aid tries to break. C is punitive. D abandons prevention.

notes.front: During an inspection you find a component that has failed in a way that could affect other aircraft of the type. Which ACS skill applies?
notes.back: A: File a Malfunction or Defect Report.
notes.explanation: The ACS Human Factors skills include filing a Malfunction or Defect Report.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.S1 File a Malfunction or Defect Report.
notes.choices:
A) File a Malfunction or Defect Report
B) Brief a shift turnover
C) Perform a tap test
D) Locate human factors information
notes.choicesExplained: B and D are other Human Factors skills that do not report the defect. C is an inspection skill.

notes.front: A technician is asked to sign a stack of task cards for work a colleague says is done. What should they do before signing each?
notes.back: D: Read each item and confirm it has been performed.
notes.explanation: Before the pen touches the paper, the technician should read the item and confirm it has been performed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Complacency”, p. 14-14
notes.evidence: Prior to the pen touching the paper for a signature, the technician should read the item before signing and confirm it has been performed.
notes.choices:
A) Sign all; the colleague is reliable
B) Sign only the easy ones
C) Sign and add “assumed complete”
D) Read each item and confirm it has been performed
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C sign for work not verified.

notes.front: How do maintenance errors typically differ from pilot errors?
notes.back: Pilot errors tend to have immediate, highly visible effects; maintenance errors tend to be more latent and less obvious.
notes.explanation: Maintenance errors can be just as lethal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Importance of Human Factors”, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: Although pilot/co-pilot errors tend to have immediate and highly visible effects, maintenance errors tend to be more latent and less obvious. However, they can be just as lethal.

notes.front: How do active and latent failures differ in Reason’s model?
notes.back: Active: effects are immediate. Latent: from a decision or action made long before, dormant until the incident.
notes.explanation: Both can be present in the same event, such as an aircraft slipping off a jack.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Human Factors”, p. 14-12
notes.evidence: There are two types of failure which can occur—active and latent. An active failure is one in which the effects are immediate.

notes.front: How do unintentional and intentional errors differ?
notes.back: Unintentional: an accidental deviation, a slip or a mistake. Intentional: knowingly doing wrong, really a violation.
notes.explanation: The difference lies in whether the person chose to deviate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Errors”, p. 14-13
notes.evidence: They did not mean to make that error but unknowingly and unintentionally did.

notes.front: How does assertiveness differ from aggression?
notes.back: Assertiveness expresses feelings, opinions, beliefs and needs in a positive, productive manner; the handbook says it should not be confused with aggression.
notes.explanation: Assertive technicians raise concerns without attacking people.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lack of Assertiveness”, p. 14-22
notes.evidence: Assertiveness is the ability to express your feelings, opinions, beliefs, and needs in a positive, productive manner and should not be confused with being aggressive.

notes.front: How do the physical and the organisational environment differ in PEAR?
notes.back: Physical: temperature, humidity, lighting, noise, cleanliness, workplace design. Organisational: cooperation, communication, shared values, respect, company culture.
notes.explanation: The organisational environment is the less tangible one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Organizational”, p. 14-10
notes.evidence: The important factors in an organizational environment are typically related to cooperation, communication, shared values, mutual respect, and the culture of the company.
